questions.prompt: On the companion's task board, which step is what guarantees that two agents never claim the same task?

options.text: The rename that moves `open/<task>` to `claimed/<task>.<agent>`.
options.feedback: The rename only moves the file so the owner is readable. On Windows two renames of one task both returned without an error, so a rename-only board double-claimed.

options.text: Checking after the rename that the destination exists and the source is gone.
options.feedback: That was the board's first repair. It narrowed the window without closing it: another rename could still change the state each check read.

options.text: Creating `.claims/<task>` with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` before the rename.
options.feedback: The exclusive create succeeds for exactly one caller and raises FileExistsError for every other; POSIX specifies the check and the creation as atomic.

options.text: Walking `open_tasks()` in sorted order.
options.feedback: The order only decides which task every agent reaches for first; it makes all of them contend for the head task rather than preventing a double claim.

questions.explanation: Exclusivity comes from the token: one path per task that only one caller can create. The rename that follows is a move, not the exclusion, which is why the companion takes the token first.
hints: Which operation is specified to fail for every caller but one?

questions.prompt: A team's task board claims by rename alone. Its threaded test drains a 400-task board with eight threads 200 times on Linux and never sees a double claim, so the team ships it to developers on every platform. Which assessment is right?

options.text: Safe: POSIX makes rename atomic, so the 200 passing runs only confirm what the specification already guarantees everywhere.
options.feedback: Atomic visibility of a name is not exclusion of a second claimer, and the board will also run on Windows, where the same race reproduced in 8 of 8 runs.

options.text: Unsafe: 200 runs is too few, and more Linux runs would eventually show the race.
options.feedback: The Linux runs in the post found none at all (0 of 8 and 0 of 20); the problem is the platform the board was not tested on, not the run count.

options.text: Unsafe on any platform: a rename can never decide which of two claimers wins.
options.feedback: On Linux, ext4, the loser's rename found its source gone and raised, so rename alone did exclude there. The trouble is that this is a property of the platform.

options.text: Unsafe beyond Linux: rename exclusivity varies by platform, so claim by an exclusive create, which is specified on both.
options.feedback: On Windows the same rename-only board handed one task to two agents in 8 of 8 runs; an exclusive create is specified to exclude on POSIX and on Windows.

questions.explanation: The post's race ran 0 of 8 and 0 of 20 on Linux and 8 of 8 on Windows. A passing test measures the platform it ran on; the claim should rest on a primitive whose exclusivity is specified everywhere it will run.
hints: Did the same rename-only board behave the same way on every platform the post measured?
What does a test on one platform say about another?

questions.prompt: Every test that first shipped with the rename-only board passed. Why could none of them have caught the double claim?

answer.model: Because every test was single-threaded: a race needs two claims to interleave, and a schedule that never interleaves cannot produce one, so only a concurrent test with threads and a barrier can see it.
accept: ^(?![\s\S]*\b(maybe|perhaps|probably|possibly|not sure|i think|might)\b)(?![\s\S]*\b(were|was|are|is)\s+(all\s+)?(multi-?threaded|concurrent|parallel|threaded)\b)(?![\s\S]*\bnot\s+single[- ]threaded\b)(?![\s\S]*\bsingle[- ]?thread\w*\s+(tests?|suites?)\s+((is|are|was|were)\s+(enough|sufficient|fine|adequate)|(can|could|do|does|would|will)\s+(catch|see|find|detect|reveal|show))\b)(?=(?:\S+\s+){3})(?=[\s\S]*\b(single[- ]?thread\w*|one thread|sequential\w*|serial\w*|no (threads|concurrency|parallelism)|not (concurrent|threaded|parallel)|never\b[\s\S]{0,30}\b(concurrent\w*|in parallel|at once|simultaneous\w*)|without (threads|concurrency)|(never|didn't|did not|don't|do not) interleav\w*|no interleaving)\b)[\s\S]*\S

questions.explanation: A race exists only in a schedule where two claims overlap. Single-threaded tests run one claim at a time, so they assert exclusivity in the one setting where it cannot fail; the companion's barrier-synchronised threaded test is the only one of its nine that could see the bug.
hints: How many claims were ever in flight at once in those tests?

questions.prompt: `claim(root, agent)` claims by rename alone and can hand one task to two agents. Fix it so that exclusivity comes from creating a token `root/.claims/<task>` with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` before the move: skip a task whose token exists, and if the move fails after the token was taken, release the token and try the next task. Keep the return value and the board layout.
questions.tests:
import tempfile
import threading
from pathlib import Path


def board(tasks):
    root = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
    for d in ("open", "claimed", ".claims"):
        (root / d).mkdir()
    for t in tasks:
        (root / "open" / t).write_text("", encoding="utf-8")
    return root


# 1. a claim takes the first task, moves it, and leaves a token keyed on the task
root = board(["task-0", "task-1"])
assert claim(root, "ada") == "task-0"
assert (root / "claimed" / "task-0.ada").exists() and not (root / "open" / "task-0").exists()
assert sorted(p.name for p in (root / ".claims").iterdir()) == ["task-0"], "the token is .claims/<task>"

# 2. a task whose token another agent already created is skipped, and stays in open/
root = board(["task-1", "task-2"])
(root / ".claims" / "task-1").write_text("", encoding="utf-8")
assert claim(root, "ada") == "task-2", "a held token must exclude the task"
assert (root / "open" / "task-1").exists()
assert claim(root, "linus") is None

# 3. when the move fails after the token was taken, the token is released and the next task is tried
root = board(["task-3", "task-4"])
(root / "claimed" / "task-3.ada").mkdir()
(root / "claimed" / "task-3.ada" / "keep").write_text("", encoding="utf-8")   # the rename cannot land here
assert claim(root, "ada") == "task-4"
assert not (root / ".claims" / "task-3").exists(), "release the token when the move fails"

# 4. eight threads behind a barrier drain 200 tasks with no task claimed twice
root = board([f"task-{i:03d}" for i in range(200)])
got, lock, gate = [], threading.Lock(), threading.Barrier(8)


def agent(name):
    gate.wait()
    while (t := claim(root, name)) is not None:
        with lock:
            got.append(t)


threads = [threading.Thread(target=agent, args=(f"a{i}",)) for i in range(8)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()
assert len(got) == 200 and len(set(got)) == 200, (len(got), len(set(got)))
assert len(list((root / "claimed").iterdir())) == 200
print("all tests passed")
questions.explanation: The token is keyed on the task, so every claimer of one task contends for one name and the exclusive create picks one winner; the rename only makes the owner readable. Releasing the token when the move fails keeps a task claimable that nobody actually took.
hints: Which `os.open` flags make a create fail when the path already exists?
Key the token on the task name, not on the agent, and catch only `FileExistsError` around the create.
Wrap the rename in its own try, and unlink the token in its except clause before continuing.

questions.prompt: Illustrative numbers: six agents each produce a verified branch every 40 minutes, and one serialised merge gate takes 10 minutes per candidate. How many branches land per hour once the swarm is running?
questions.precision_note: $\min(60 \times 6 / 40,\ 60 / 10) = \min(9, 6) = 6$, the closed form `landings_per_hour` of snippets/gate_ceiling.py. The production rate alone (9) ignores the gate.
questions.explanation: The agents produce $6 \times 60 / 40 = 9$ branches an hour, but the gate clears only $60 / 10 = 6$; past $N^* = T/G = 4$ agents the gate sets the rate, and the extra branches queue.
hints: Compute what the agents produce per hour and what the gate can clear per hour.
Sustained landings are the smaller of the two.

questions.prompt: A team lands 2,016 merges a week through one serialised merge gate, spread evenly over all 168 hours. At most how many minutes can the gate spend on each candidate?
questions.precision_note: $2{,}016 / 168 = 12$ landings an hour, so $60 / 12 = 5$ minutes each; the same arithmetic snippets/gate_ceiling.py applies to the reported Stripe figure ($1{,}300 / 168 = 7.74$ an hour, 7.75 minutes). Spreading over a 40-hour working week instead gives 1.19 minutes.
questions.explanation: Around the clock the gate must clear 12 candidates an hour, one every five minutes. Any slower and the queue grows without bound, whatever the number of agents.
hints: Find the landings per hour first.
Divide the minutes in an hour by that rate.

questions.prompt: Illustrative numbers: each agent fails a task independently with probability 0.02. A round runs 20 tasks in parallel. What is the probability, in percent, that the round contains at least one failure? Give one decimal.
questions.precision_note: $1 - 0.98^{20} = 1 - 0.6676 = 0.3324$, the closed form of snippets/gate_ceiling.py. Adding the probabilities ($20 \times 0.02 = 40\%$) or using one task (2%) falls outside the tolerance.
questions.explanation: The chance of no failure in the round is $0.98^{20} = 0.668$, so a third of rounds contain a casualty even though each agent fails only one task in fifty; at swarm scale reclaim is the ordinary path, not a contingency.
hints: Compute the probability that no task fails first.
Subtract it from one.

questions.prompt: Put the life of one claim on a board with leases in order, from the moment an agent reaches for a task to the moment a dead holder's task is claimed again.

items.text: Stamp the claim file's modification time with `os.utime`.
The sweeper finds the lease expired, moves the claim back to `open/<task>`, and only then deletes `.claims/<task>`.
Another agent's exclusive create of `.claims/<task>` succeeds, and the task is claimed again.

questions.explanation: The token comes first because it is the exclusion; the rename makes the owner readable; the stamp starts the lease, which the rename alone would not, because a rename keeps the old modification time. The sweeper moves the claim back and releases the token last; until the token is gone, every agent's exclusive create on it fails, so the next claim comes only after both steps.
hints: Which step decides who owns the task, and which only records it?
Can the lease be stamped on a file before it exists at its claimed path?

questions.prompt: Match each deployment to the isolation and claim primitive that fits it.

left.text: One machine, one filesystem, tasks the team trusts
One machine, but tasks that run code the agents wrote and may be destructive

right.text: A git worktree per agent; claim by exclusive create in the board directory
A clone of a bare upstream per agent; claim by pushing a lock file
A container per task with a clone inside it
One shared checkout for every agent, with a lock server for claims

questions.explanation: Worktrees and a local exclusive create need one filesystem; across machines git's rejected push is the compare-and-set; destructive tasks need process and network isolation, which a worktree does not give. A shared checkout lets agents clobber each other's edits whatever the claim.
hints: Ask first whether the agents share a filesystem, then whether file isolation is enough.

questions.prompt: What does a fresh `git worktree add` give the agent that will work in it?

options.text: A full copy of the repository's history, so it is independent of the main checkout.
options.feedback: Worktrees share one object database; a worktree costs a working copy, not a copy of the history.

options.text: Tracked files on its own branch, and nothing else: no installed dependencies, no `.env`.
options.feedback: A worktree is a fresh checkout; each one needs its own dependency install and gitignored configuration.

options.text: A copy of the main checkout's working directory, including its virtual environment and `.env`.
options.feedback: Untracked and gitignored files are not carried over; Claude Code adds `.worktreeinclude` to copy chosen ones.

options.text: A sandbox that isolates the agent's processes and network from the other agents.
options.feedback: A worktree isolates files and nothing else: processes, network and credentials stay shared.

questions.explanation: A worktree is a separate working copy of tracked files on its own branch, sharing the repository's history. The setup it lacks, not disk space, is the marginal cost of another agent.
hints: Is a gitignored file tracked?

questions.prompt: A harness creates each agent's worktree with `git worktree add <path> <branch>`, and when that fails it retries the same command with `--force` appended. What does the retry risk?

options.text: Nothing: the exclusive claim already keeps agents on different tasks, so branches cannot collide.
options.feedback: The claim keeps tasks apart, not branches; a retry that reuses a branch name puts two agents on it.

options.text: It deletes the existing worktree and the uncommitted work in it, then creates the new worktree in its place.
options.feedback: `add --force` does not remove another worktree; it overrides the checks that would have refused the add.

options.text: Nothing, because git refuses a branch checked out elsewhere even with `--force`.
options.feedback: That refusal is exactly what `--force` overrides, in the manual's words, "these safeguards".

options.text: Two agents checked out on one branch, because `--force` overrides the refusal that would have stopped it.
options.feedback: By default `add` refuses a branch already checked out in another worktree; `--force` turns that guarantee off. Retry with a new branch name instead.

questions.explanation: The refusal to check out one branch twice is a free correctness guarantee, and an automated retry with `--force` turns it off for every agent at once.
hints: What does the manual say `--force` overrides?
Which refusal was the first attempt likely to hit?

questions.prompt: Branch A renames `parse_expr` and updates its seven callers; branch B adds an eighth call to `parse_expr`. Both suites pass and git merges them with no textual conflict. What catches the break before it reaches the mainline?

options.text: Running each branch's suite again before landing it.
options.feedback: Each branch is green on its own; the broken state exists in neither branch, only in their combination.

options.text: Building the candidate merge and running the suite on it, landing only if green.
options.feedback: The semantic conflict exists only in the merged result, so the gate must test that result.

options.text: Git's merge, which refuses two hunks that touch the same function name in one file.
options.feedback: Git sees two disjoint hunks and merges them without a murmur; it does not read the code's meaning.

options.text: Smaller branches, which make conflicts of this kind impossible.
options.feedback: Conflicts scale with overlap in the decomposition, not with branch size; two tiny branches can still clash this way.

questions.explanation: A semantic conflict is a merge git accepts and the mainline rejects; only a gate on the merged result sees it, which is why the merge, not the work, is serialised.
hints: In which tree does the broken call exist?

questions.prompt: A lease sweeper reads each claim file's modification time. Why must the agent stamp the claim file with `os.utime` when it claims, rather than rely on the rename?

answer.model: Because a rename keeps the file's old modification time, so a task that waited in open/ longer than the lease would look expired the moment it was claimed and the sweeper would reclaim it at once.

questions.explanation: `os.rename` moves a file without changing its modification time, so a claim inherits the age of the task. Without the stamp, a task that sat in `open/` for longer than the lease is reclaimed the moment anyone takes it; the claimer stamps the lease at claim time and again to renew.
hints: What happens to a file's modification time when it is renamed?
How old would a fresh claim look to the sweeper if the task had waited an hour?

questions.prompt: A lease sweeper moves an expired claim from `claimed/task-9.ada` back to `open/task-9` and records the attempt, but never deletes `.claims/task-9`. What does the board do with task-9 from then on?

options.text: Two agents can now claim it at the same time, because the stale token confuses every later exclusive create.
options.feedback: A held token makes every exclusive create on it fail; it can only stop claims, never admit two.

options.text: It sits in `open/` forever: every agent's exclusive create on the token fails, so nobody can claim it.
options.feedback: The token still exists, so every claimer gets FileExistsError and skips the task: quarantined by accident.

options.text: The sweeper reclaims it again on its next pass and eventually quarantines it.
options.feedback: The sweeper walks `claimed/`, and task-9 never returns there, so its attempt counter never moves again.

options.text: The next agent's claim raises an exception, which stops that agent.
options.feedback: The claim loop catches FileExistsError and moves on to the next task; the failure is silent.

questions.explanation: The exclusive create refuses a task whose token exists. A reclaim that does not release the token leaves the task visible in `open/` and unclaimable, a silent loss of work, which is why the sweeper deletes the token after the move.
hints: What does `claim` do when the token's create raises FileExistsError?
Which directory does the sweeper walk?

questions.prompt: A swarm's merge gate already plays the role of post 11's verification gate: it lands a branch only if the candidate merge passes. Extend it so that a reclaimed task cannot land twice. Explain why the ownership check in `complete()` is not enough on its own, what the gate must know about each branch, what it keeps, and what it refuses.
questions.solution:
**Why `complete()` is not enough.** It refuses a completion from an agent that no longer holds the claim, which protects the board, but the late agent's work has already been done: its branch exists and can reach the gate. The check is also made before acting, and Kleppmann's argument applies: a check on the lock just before writing cannot fix a process paused between the check and the write.

**What the gate must know.** Every claim carries a generation: the attempt number the sweeper's tally already counts, incremented on each reclaim. The agent carries it on its branch (in the branch name or a trailer).

**What the gate keeps.** For each task, the highest generation it has seen or landed.

**What it refuses.** A branch whose generation is lower than the highest seen for its task, as a stale duplicate, discarded rather than reported as a failure; this is Kleppmann's fencing token, with the resource rejecting writes whose token has gone backwards. The verification part is unchanged: the candidate merge must still pass, because it is the gate that decides, not the agent's report.

**What remains.** Execution is still at least once: the loser's tokens are spent. The effect is single.

rubric.criterion: Explains that `complete()` protects the board, not the work, and that a check before acting can go stale
Uses an increasing claim generation carried on the branch
The gate keeps the highest generation per task and refuses lower ones as duplicates
Keeps post 11's rule that the gate's check on the merged result decides, and states that execution stays at least once

questions.explanation: The fencing token moves the check from the agent to the resource, here the merge gate, which is the only place where every agent's work meets; the verification gate of post 11 gains a second refusal, a stale generation, beside a failing check.
hints: Where does the late agent's work go after its `complete()` is refused?
Kleppmann's fix pushes the check down to the resource; what is the resource in a swarm, and what number would it compare?

questions.prompt: The post's lease uses the claim file's modification time on one shared filesystem. Design leases, reclaim and fencing for the many-machine swarm instead, where each agent claims by pushing a lock file to a bare upstream repository and nothing shares a filesystem or a clock. Say how a lease is taken and renewed, who reclaims and how, how duplicates are kept off the mainline, and what still runs twice.
questions.solution:
**Taking and renewing.** The lock file is the lease: the agent commits `current_tasks/<task>` with its name, a generation number and an expiry written as a time from the upstream's point of view (or a commit count), and pushes; git rejects the push that does not fast-forward, so one agent wins. Renewal is another commit to the same file, pushed. Agents' clocks cannot be trusted to agree, so the expiry is read against one clock: the sweeper's, or the upstream host's commit times.

**Reclaim.** One sweeper (or any agent, serialised by the same push rule) reads `current_tasks/`, finds locks whose last renewal is older than the lease, and commits their removal together with an increment of the task's attempt count; quarantine is a move of the task file into `quarantine/` after N attempts. The push rule makes the reclaim a compare-and-set: if the holder renewed in the meantime, the sweeper's push is rejected and it re-reads.

**Fencing.** The generation in the lock increases on every reclaim. The merge gate keeps the highest generation per task and refuses a branch carrying a lower one, so a woken agent's push cannot land a stale copy; the gate still tests the candidate merge before landing.

**What still runs twice.** The work of a slow agent reclaimed while alive; only its effect is fenced. Making tasks idempotent keeps the cost of that duplicate to its tokens. The price of the design is a round trip per claim, renewal and reclaim, and a board every agent sees slightly stale.

rubric.criterion: A lease taken and renewed through pushed commits, with the rejected non-fast-forward push as the compare-and-set
Expiry judged against one clock rather than each agent's own
A reclaim that is itself a compare-and-set and increments an attempt count, with quarantine
A generation fenced at the merge gate, which still tests the merged result
States honestly that work can still run twice, and what the design costs

questions.explanation: On many machines the push replaces the exclusive create as the compare-and-set, so leases, reclaims and fences all become commits that race through the same rejected push, and the merge gate remains the resource that fences duplicates.
hints: Which operation plays the exclusive create's role when nothing shares a filesystem?
Whose clock decides that a lease has expired?
Where does the fencing token get checked?

questions.prompt: In the snippet's run, agent A woke after agent B had finished task-7, did the same work, and left `settings.toml` unchanged. Which property made A's second execution harmless?

options.text: The ownership check in `complete()`, which refused agent A's completion after B finished.
options.feedback: The refusal came after A had already written; it kept the board right but did not stop the work's effect.

options.text: The lease, which expired while A was quiet.
options.feedback: The expiry is what let the task run twice in the first place; it does not make the rerun harmless.

options.text: The work's idempotence: it made the file hold the spec rather than appending to it.
options.feedback: An "ensure the file matches the spec" task run twice is the same as once, so A's late run found nothing to change.

options.text: The exclusive create, which stopped A and B holding the task together.
options.feedback: They never held it together, yet the task still ran twice: exclusivity in time does not give exactly-once.

questions.explanation: At-least-once execution is settled for, and the second run made harmless. Idempotent work is the cheapest way; the ownership check protects the board, and a fence at the gate protects the mainline.
hints: Which of these acted on the file itself?

questions.prompt: With the snippet's rule, a claim is reclaimed when `now - mtime >= LEASE_S`, and `LEASE_S = 900`. A holder stamps its claim at t = 0 and renews it at t = 250, then dies. The sweeper runs at t = 600, 900, 1,200 and 1,500. At which sweep, in simulated seconds, is the task reclaimed?

stimulus.content:
if EPOCH + now - claim.stat().st_mtime < LEASE_S:
    continue                                  # holder is still inside its lease

questions.precision_note: The last stamp is 250, so the lease runs to $250 + 900 = 1{,}150$; at 900 the age is 650, still inside; at 1,200 it is 950, past it. Counting from the first stamp (0) gives 900, which is wrong because the renewal reset the lease.
questions.explanation: A renewal restarts the lease, so expiry is 900 seconds after the last stamp, t = 1,150; the first sweep at or after it is t = 1,200.
hints: Which stamp does the sweeper see?
Find the first sweep at least 900 seconds after it.
